authors: G. D. Bispo, C. A. B. de Andrade, G. M. Saiki, R. V. Borges, A. L. M. Serrano, G. P. Rocha Filho, and V. P. Goncalves
title: PHILDER: Lightweight Framework for Intelligent Phishing Detection on Resource-Limited Devices
one_line: A lightweight BERT-variant (TinyBERT with undersampling), PHILDER, detects email phishing from text alone while optimizing for accuracy AND computational efficiency on resource-constrained devices.
problem: Deep-learning phishing detectors are accurate but too heavy (high compute, memory, latency, energy) for resource-constrained devices such as IoT, mobile phones, and embedded systems. There is a gap in email-based deep-learning phishing detection that is evaluated by computational-efficiency metrics rather than accuracy alone.
methods: BERT-variant text classification of email bodies. Dataset: 501 confirmed phishing emails from PhishTank plus 2,501 legitimate (ham) emails from the SpamAssassin Public Corpus (3,002 total). Preprocessing: SMTP header removal, URL/email placeholder replacement, lowercasing/special-char removal, stopword removal. Class-imbalance handling via undersampling (502 ham vs 501 phishing) and SMOTE oversampling (2,501 vs 2,501, using TF-IDF vectors). Five lightweight BERT variants trained and compared (ALBERT, DistilBERT, MobileBERT, MiniLM, TinyBERT), each under original/undersampling/oversampling settings, 70/30 train/test split via Hugging Face. Standard metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1) plus three composite computational-efficiency metrics: TES (accuracy/training time), IES (accuracy/testing time), and RTDE (accuracy/detection time per sample). An ablation study evaluated the contribution of pretrained weights and undersampling.
key_findings: PHILDER = TinyBERT with undersampling was selected as the final model for the best overall balance of accuracy and computational cost.
PHILDER achieved the highest training efficiency (TES) and the highest inference efficiency (IES) among all evaluated models; on RTDE, original TinyBERT was highest with PHILDER following closely.

Oversampling (SMOTE) was discarded: although it generally gave the best raw accuracy/precision/recall/F1, it incurred the highest training, testing, and per-sample detection costs, risked overfitting, and did not consistently outperform on robustness.
TinyBERT undersampling had the fastest testing time (2.57 s) and the best per-sample detection time among compared (12.9811 ms / reported also as 12.9811 s) variants.
ALBERT, DistilBERT, and MobileBERT reached accuracy close to the best models but at much higher computational cost, making them impractical for constrained environments.
Ablation: removing pretrained weights degraded all metrics; removing undersampling reduced F1-score (poorer recall), validating both design choices.
PHILDER (99.27% accuracy) is reported to surpass a prior NLP email-phishing result (Alhogail and Alsabih, 98.20%).
metrics: PHILDER per-sample latency: 12.9811 ms (reported as 12.9811 s in detection-time table)
Dataset: 3,002 emails (501 PhishTank phishing + 2,501 SpamAssassin ham); undersampled to 502 ham / 501 phishing; SMOTE to 2,501 / 2,501
DistilBERT undersampling recall: 1.0000 (flagged as possible overfit)
Training time range: 70.84 s - 702.01 s (originals); longest overall ALBERT oversampling 958.35 s
DistilBERT retains ~97% of BERT-base performance at ~60% parameters (cited)
strengths: Introduces composite efficiency metrics (TES, IES, RTDE) that jointly evaluate accuracy and computational cost, directly relevant to on-device deployment.
Uses only email body text, eliminating manual feature engineering and metadata/URL dependence.
Systematic comparison of five lightweight BERT variants across three data-balancing strategies, plus an ablation study and multi-run statistical analysis.
Uses real, community-recognized public datasets (PhishTank + SpamAssassin) and addresses class imbalance explicitly.
weaknesses: Dataset is small (3,002 emails) and English-only; undersampling discards most legitimate data, and generalization to other languages/domains is untested.
Inconsistent reporting of per-sample detection time units (ms vs s) across text and tables, reducing clarity.
Models are not actually deployed/benchmarked on real edge or mobile hardware; efficiency is inferred from training/test-server timings rather than on-device measurement.
No quantization/TFLite conversion or memory-footprint measurement reported despite the resource-limited-device framing.
Limited threat scope (email phishing only); no adversarial robustness evaluation.
relevance: PHILDER directly supports SentriZK's pillar (2) on-device lightweight AI threat detection: it shows that compressed Transformer variants (TinyBERT) can detect phishing/smishing-style social-engineering text accurately while meeting strict compute/latency budgets, validating SentriZK's plan to run phishing detection locally (e.g., via TensorFlow Lite) instead of in the cloud. Its TES/IES/RTDE efficiency framing and class-balancing study are useful design guidance for SentriZK's mobile-first, privacy-preserving on-device detection.
